rows.stem: If A and B are two square matrices of the same order, then \((A + B)(A - B)\) is equal to :
rows.solution:
Expand using the distributive law, but keep the order of every product, because matrix multiplication is not commutative:

\((A + B)(A - B) = A(A - B) + B(A - B) = A^2 - AB + BA - B^2\).

The two middle terms are \(-AB\) and \(+BA\), and they cancel only when \(AB = BA\), which is not given. So the expansion is \(A^2 - AB + BA - B^2\), and the familiar scalar identity \(A^2 - B^2\) does not hold for matrices in general.

rows.stem: If a matrix A is both symmetric and skew-symmetric, then A is a :
rows.solution: Let \(A' \) denote the transpose of \(A\). Symmetric means \(A' = A\); skew-symmetric means \(A' = -A\). If both hold at once, then \(A = A' = -A\), so \(2A = O\) and hence \(A = O\). Therefore the only matrix that is both symmetric and skew-symmetric is the zero matrix. (Working entry by entry gives the same thing: \(a_{ij} = a_{ji}\) and \(a_{ij} = -a_{ji}\) force \(2a_{ij} = 0\), so every entry vanishes.)

rows.stem: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\cos 2x}{\sin^2 x \cos^2 x}\ dx\) is equal to :
rows.solution:
Write \(\cos 2x = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x\) and split the fraction:

\(\frac{\cos 2x}{\sin^2 x \cos^2 x} = \frac{\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x}{\sin^2 x \cos^2 x} = \frac{\cos^2 x}{\sin^2 x \cos^2 x} - \frac{\sin^2 x}{\sin^2 x \cos^2 x} = \frac{1}{\sin^2 x} - \frac{1}{\cos^2 x} = \operatorname{cosec}^2 x - \sec^2 x\).

Integrating term by term, and using \(\int \operatorname{cosec}^2 x\,dx = -\cot x\) and \(\int \sec^2 x\,dx = \tan x\):

\(\int \frac{\cos 2x}{\sin^2 x \cos^2 x}\,dx = -\cot x - \tan x + C = -(\cot x + \tan x) + C\).

So the integral equals \(-(\cot x + \tan x) + C\); differentiating any of the other three forms gives \(\sec^2 x - \operatorname{cosec}^2 x\) or a mixed sign combination, none of which is the integrand.

rows.subtopic: Definite Integrals and the Fundamental Theorem
rows.stem: If \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} \dfrac{1}{1 + 4x^2}\ dx = \dfrac{\pi}{8}\), then the value of 'a' is :
rows.solution:
First evaluate the integral. Using \(\int \frac{dx}{1 + (kx)^2} = \frac{1}{k}\tan^{-1}(kx)\) with \(k = 2\),

\(\int\limits_0^a \frac{dx}{1 + 4x^2} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\tan^{-1}(2x)\right]_0^a = \frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}(2a)\).

Setting this equal to \(\frac{\pi}{8}\) gives \(\tan^{-1}(2a) = \frac{\pi}{4}\), so \(2a = \tan\frac{\pi}{4} = 1\) and \(a = \frac{1}{2}\).

So the value of \('a'\) is \(\frac{1}{2}\). (Checking the other choices: \(a = \frac{1}{4}\) gives \(\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{2}\), \(a = \frac{1}{8}\) gives \(\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{4}\) and \(a = 4\) gives \(\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1} 8\) — none of which is \(\frac{\pi}{8}\).)

rows.stem: The integrating factor of the differential equation \(\dfrac{dx}{dy} = \dfrac{x \log x}{\dfrac{2}{x} \log x - y}\) is :
rows.solution:
The equation is given as \(\frac{dx}{dy}\), so first turn it the right way up. Taking reciprocals,

\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{2}{x}\log x - y}{x \log x} = \frac{2\log x}{x^2 \log x} - \frac{y}{x\log x} = \frac{2}{x^2} - \frac{y}{x \log x}\).

Rearranged into the standard linear form \(\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q\),

\(\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{y}{x \log x} = \frac{2}{x^2}\), so \(P = \frac{1}{x \log x}\).

For the integrating factor, note \(\int \frac{dx}{x \log x} = \log|\log x|\) (substitute \(u = \log x\), \(du = \frac{dx}{x}\)). Hence

\(\text{I.F.} = e^{\int P\,dx} = e^{\log|\log x|} = \log x\).

So the integrating factor is \(\log x\).

rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.solution:
\(\sec^{-1} u\) is defined only when \(|u| \ge 1\), i.e. its domain is \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\).

So we need \(|2x + 1| \ge 1\), which splits into two cases:

\(2x + 1 \le -1 \Rightarrow 2x \le -2 \Rightarrow x \le -1\), or \(2x + 1 \ge 1 \Rightarrow 2x \ge 0 \Rightarrow x \ge 0\).

Hence the domain is \((-\infty, -1] \cup [0, \infty)\), i.e. all real \(x\) except those with \(-1 < x < 0\).

rows.stem: The radius of a cylinder is decreasing at a rate of 2 cm/s and the altitude is increasing at the rate of 3 cm/s. Find the rate of change of volume of this cylinder when its radius is 4 cm and altitude is 6 cm.
rows.solution:
Let \(r\), \(h\) and \(V\) be the radius, altitude and volume of the cylinder at time \(t\). We are given \(\frac{dr}{dt} = -2\) cm/s (decreasing) and \(\frac{dh}{dt} = 3\) cm/s (increasing), and we want \(\frac{dV}{dt}\) when \(r = 4\) cm and \(h = 6\) cm.

Here BOTH \(r\) and \(h\) vary, so differentiate \(V = \pi r^2 h\) as a product:

\(\frac{dV}{dt} = \pi\left(2r\,\frac{dr}{dt}\,h + r^2\,\frac{dh}{dt}\right)\).

Substituting \(r = 4\), \(h = 6\), \(\frac{dr}{dt} = -2\), \(\frac{dh}{dt} = 3\):

\(\frac{dV}{dt} = 2\pi(4)(-2)(6) + \pi(4)^2(3) = -96\pi + 48\pi = -48\pi\ \text{cm}^3/\text{s}\).

The sign is negative, so the volume is decreasing at the rate of \(48\pi\ \text{cm}^3/\text{s}\) (about \(150{\cdot}8\ \text{cm}^3/\text{s}\)).

rows.stem: Show that \(f(x) = \tan^{-1}(\sin x + \cos x)\) is an increasing function in \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]\).
rows.solution:
\(f(x) = \tan^{-1}(\sin x + \cos x)\). Differentiating with the chain rule, and using \(\frac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}u = \frac{1}{1 + u^2}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}\) with \(u = \sin x + \cos x\):

\(f'(x) = \frac{1}{1 + (\sin x + \cos x)^2}\,(\cos x - \sin x)\).

The denominator \(1 + (\sin x + \cos x)^2\) is at least \(1\), so it is positive for every \(x\); the sign of \(f'\) is therefore the sign of \(\cos x - \sin x\).

On \(\left[0, \frac{\pi}{4}\right]\) we have \(0 \le x \le \frac{\pi}{4}\), where \(\cos x \ge \sin x\) (they are equal only at the right endpoint \(x = \frac{\pi}{4}\)). Hence \(\cos x - \sin x \ge 0\) throughout, so

\(f'(x) \ge 0\) for all \(x \in \left[0, \frac{\pi}{4}\right]\),

and therefore \(f\) is an increasing function on \(\left[0, \frac{\pi}{4}\right]\).

rows.stem: Find the particular solution of the differential equation \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} - \dfrac{y}{x} + \operatorname{cosec}\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) = 0\); given that \(y = 0\), when \(x = 1\).
rows.solution:
The equation \(\frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{y}{x} + \operatorname{cosec}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = 0\), i.e.

\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{x} - \operatorname{cosec}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)\),

has a right-hand side depending on \(x\) and \(y\) only through \(\frac{y}{x}\), so it is homogeneous.

Put \(y = vx\), so that \(\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}\). Substituting,

\(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = v - \operatorname{cosec} v \Rightarrow x\frac{dv}{dx} = -\operatorname{cosec} v\).

Separating the variables,

\(-\sin v\,dv = \frac{dx}{x}\).

Integrating both sides, \(\int(-\sin v)\,dv = \int \frac{dx}{x}\) gives

\(\cos v = \log|x| + c\), i.e. \(\cos\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = \log|x| + c\).

Applying the initial condition \(y = 0\) when \(x = 1\): then \(\frac{y}{x} = 0\), so \(\cos 0 = \log 1 + c\), i.e. \(1 = 0 + c\) and \(c = 1\).

Hence the particular solution is \(\cos\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = \log|x| + 1\).

rows.stem: Draw a rough sketch of the curve \(y = \sqrt{x}\). Using integration, find the area of the region bounded by the curve \(y = \sqrt{x}\), \(x = 4\) and x-axis, in the first quadrant.
rows.solution:
Sketch: \(y = \sqrt{x}\) is the upper half of the parabola \(y^2 = x\). It starts at the origin and rises steadily to the right, passing through \((1, 1)\) and \((4, 2)\); the line \(x = 4\) is a vertical line meeting the curve at \((4, 2)\). The region asked for lies in the first quadrant, bounded above by the curve, below by the x-axis, and on the right by \(x = 4\).

A vertical strip at abscissa \(x\) runs from \(y = 0\) up to \(y = \sqrt{x}\), and \(x\) runs from \(0\) to \(4\). Hence

\(\text{Area} = \int\limits_0^4 \sqrt{x}\,dx = \int\limits_0^4 x^{1/2}\,dx = \left[\frac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_0^4 = \frac{2}{3}\left(4^{3/2} - 0\right) = \frac{2}{3}\times 8 = \frac{16}{3}\).

So the required area is \(\frac{16}{3}\) square units.

rows.stem: An amount of ₹ 10,000 is put into three investments at the rate of 10%, 12% and 15% per annum. The combined annual income of all three investments is ₹ 1,310, however the combined annual income of the first and the second investments is ₹ 190 short of the income from the third. Use matrix method and find the investment amount in each at the beginning of the year.
rows.solution:
Let \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) (in ₹) be the amounts invested at \(10\%\), \(12\%\) and \(15\%\) respectively.

The three pieces of information give:

\(x + y + z = 10000\);

\(\frac{10}{100}x + \frac{12}{100}y + \frac{15}{100}z = 1310\), i.e. \(10x + 12y + 15z = 131000\);

the first two incomes fall \(190\) short of the third, i.e. \(\frac{15}{100}z - \left(\frac{10}{100}x + \frac{12}{100}y\right) = 190\), i.e. \(-10x - 12y + 15z = 19000\).

Write this as \(AX = B\) with

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 10 & 12 & 15 \\ -10 & -12 & 15 \end{bmatrix}\), \(X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 10000 \\ 131000 \\ 19000 \end{bmatrix}\).

Expanding along the first row, \(|A| = 1(180 + 180) - 1(150 + 150) + 1(-120 + 120) = 360 - 300 + 0 = 60 \ne 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists and the solution is unique.

Computing the cofactors and transposing,

\(\operatorname{adj} A = \begin{bmatrix} 360 & -27 & 3 \\ -300 & 25 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{60}\begin{bmatrix} 360 & -27 & 3 \\ -300 & 25 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

Hence \(X = A^{-1}B = \frac{1}{60}\begin{bmatrix} 360 & -27 & 3 \\ -300 & 25 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 10000 \\ 131000 \\ 19000 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2000 \\ 3000 \\ 5000 \end{bmatrix}\).

So the investments are ₹ 2,000 at \(10\%\), ₹ 3,000 at \(12\%\) and ₹ 5,000 at \(15\%\).

Check: the total is ₹ 10,000; the annual incomes are \(200 + 360 + 750 = 1310\), i.e. ₹ 1,310; and \(750 - (200 + 360) = 190\), so the first two together fall ₹ 190 short of the third, as required.
